sections.h2: La Paz County at a glance
sections.html:
La Paz County is a large, thinly settled county on Arizona's western edge with a small tax base. It covers 4,514 square miles and had 16,557 residents in the 2020 census. Parker is the seat and the largest town, and Quartzsite is the only other incorporated town. The Colorado River Indian Reservation lies in the western part of the county.

The 2020 census counted 13,457 housing units, of which 45.2% were vacant, and 71.8% of occupied homes were owner-occupied. Mobile homes make up part of the stock, and the Assessor's office keeps mobile home records. It updates ownership from Motor Vehicle Division title records and cannot change the owner on the roll until a new title is issued. If the old owner is still on the title, the old owner still gets the notice of value and the tax bill. Before you sell a mobile home, confirm the title has moved.

Two county offices split the work. The La Paz County Assessor values property and keeps ownership, parcel maps, exemptions, mobile homes and business personal property. The La Paz County Treasurer mails the bills and collects the money. The Assessor does not set tax rates, issue bills, or collect or refund taxes, so a question about an amount due goes to the Treasurer and a question about value goes to the Assessor.

  • Treasurer: 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 203, Parker, AZ 85344. Open Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., closed Fridays.
  • Assessor: 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 204, Parker, AZ 85344, phone 928-669-6165.
  • Recorder: records deeds and answers fee questions at 928-669-6136.

The Assessor gets deed information from the Recorder and permit information from La Paz County Community Development, the Town of Parker and the Town of Quartzsite. A house that gains a room or loses a roof without a permit can still show up on the roll later, so keep your permit paperwork in the sale file.

Half of the tax is due on October 1 and the other half on March 1 (A.R.S. 42-18052). The Treasurer sets the delinquency hour at 6:00 p.m., and postmarked payments are accepted. The smallest payment taken is $10 or 10% of the tax due, whichever is greater.

DateWhat happens
October 1First half due. Bills go out by mail in September.
Early November, 6:00 p.m.First half delinquent
December 31, 2026Last day to pay the full year and avoid interest
March 1, 2027Second half due
May 4, 2027, 6:00 p.m.Second half delinquent

If the first half is still unpaid, interest is already running. Paying the whole year by December 31 stops further interest under A.R.S. 42-18053, so a seller who closes in December can clear it at the table.

Unpaid taxes bear interest at 16% a year, simple, from the delinquency date, and a fraction of a month counts as a whole month (A.R.S. 42-18053). The Treasurer prorates the same 16% monthly from the first day of the month until the tax is paid.

  • No interest is collected if the delinquency came from an error by the assessor or treasurer.
  • No interest is collected if the full-year tax is paid on or before December 31 of the tax year.
  • The treasurer may waive interest and penalties once per property for a delinquency in the year after a mortgage or deed of trust is released, if the board of supervisors approves.

Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure good through your expected closing date. Parcel lookup and card payments run through the Treasurer's website. A card payment carries a convenience fee of $4.00 on a Visa debit card or 2.55% on a credit card, and the jurisdiction code to give by phone is 1312.

File a petition with the County Assessor within 60 days after the Assessor mailed your notice of value. The deadline is in A.R.S. 42-16051, and a postmark counts as the filing date. Notices go out each year to the owner of record. Only the full cash value or the property class can be appealed.

The petition must state your opinion of full cash value and give substantial information to support it. The statute names three methods: the income approach, the market approach (with at least one comparable property or the sale of the subject property), and the cost approach. A recent arm's-length sale of your own house is the strongest comparable you can offer.

Limited property value is separate. Proposition 117 caps its growth at 5% a year, with exceptions listed in A.R.S. Title 42, Chapter 13, Article 7. Because bills run on limited value, a jump in full cash value does not always raise your tax by the same amount.

Two programs are run through the Assessor, and the office can give you the current income and value limits. Call 928-669-6165 before you list.

  • Exemption for widows, widowers and totally disabled persons age 17 or over. You must live in Arizona, meet income requirements, and stay under an indexed assessed-value limit. A disability claim needs a physician's certification that the disability is total and permanent.
  • Senior Property Valuation Protection, often called the senior freeze. It freezes limited property value for three years. You must be 65 at the time of application, use the home as your primary Arizona residence, and meet income rules.

A value can jump when a buyer takes over a home whose prior owner held a senior freeze, so a buyer should expect a first notice of value that looks higher than the seller's. Owners of short-term rentals should also look at the rental registration form on the Assessor's page and the state's online lodging marketplace registration.

Property tax is a lien on the house that attaches on January 1 of the tax year (A.R.S. 42-17153). It outranks other liens except those held by the state and tax liens from other years, and it stays until the taxes, penalties, charges and interest are paid, a tax sale vests title in a buyer, or a certificate of removal and abatement is issued. A buyer's title company will therefore expect the current year and any back years to be paid from your proceeds.

Selling a house with tax due is routine when the numbers are clear. Work through it in this order:

  1. Get a payoff from the Treasurer for your closing date.
  2. Confirm the owner of record with the Assessor.
  3. Give both numbers to the title company.
  4. Sign the deed with its sworn affidavit of property value under A.R.S. 11-1133, which the recorder must refuse to record without, unless an exemption is noted.

The Recorder's rules are on its website: paper 8 1/2 inches wide and 11 to 14 inches long, a two-inch top margin on the first page, original ink signatures, and the right fee. Ask for the fee schedule at 928-669-6136. A cash buyer skips a lender's timeline, so the county payoff is often the only open item.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay the first half of my La Paz County tax?
faqs.a: It becomes delinquent and interest of 16% a year starts to accrue. Paying the full year on or before December 31, 2026 stops further interest under A.R.S. 42-18053.

faqs.q: Where do I pay La Paz County property tax?
faqs.a: Pay the County Treasurer at 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 203, Parker, Arizona 85344, by mail or in person, or pay online or by phone. The office is open Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., and closed Fridays. Card payments add a $4.00 fee on Visa debit or 2.55% on credit cards.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my La Paz County notice of value?
faqs.a: Sixty days from the date the Assessor mailed the notice. Your petition goes to the County Assessor, and a postmark counts as the filing date under A.R.S. 42-16051.

faqs.q: Does La Paz County have a senior property tax freeze?
faqs.a: Yes. Senior Property Valuation Protection freezes limited property value for three years. The owner must be 65 at application, use the home as a primary Arizona residence, and meet income limits. Call the Assessor at 928-669-6165 for the form and current limits.

faqs.q: Can I sell a La Paz County house that still has tax due?
faqs.a: Yes. The lien is paid from your proceeds at closing. Get a payoff from the Treasurer for your closing date, since interest runs monthly on delinquent amounts, and give it to the title company.
